title: The Professional Poker-Face Trap
hook: Many men learn at work to show nothing, and then discover that a face which gives nothing away also invites nobody in.
why:
In many workplaces, a still face is treated as a professional virtue. Traders, lawyers, surgeons, police officers, managers and salesmen learn to keep their reactions to themselves: not to flinch at bad news, not to look pleased too early, not to let a client or a rival see what they think. Composure has real uses. But many men carry it everywhere, into every meeting and conversation, until a face that was meant to protect them starts to cost them.

This chapter is about that cost. It covers where the professional poker face comes from; the evidence that expressive people are trusted more; how other people use your face as information, and what they assume when there is none; the trade-off between warmth and competence in a smile; what happens when the face is wrong for the moment, as in a corporate apology; the toll of acting all day; and how to be selectively expressive, keeping composure for the moments that need it. The chapter on the mask in Part II looked at hiding distress; this one looks at the everyday face of work.

teach.h: Where the poker face comes from.
teach.p:
Few men decide to have a poker face. They learn it. Some learn it at home, from fathers who did not show feelings. Some learn it at school, where showing hurt invited more of it. Many learn it at work, in cultures that equate a still face with strength, control and seniority, and that punish visible doubt, frustration or enthusiasm as unprofessional.

The chapter on reading yourself under stress in Part VI described the psychologist Ronald Levant's argument that many boys are taught to stop noticing and naming soft feelings. The professional poker face is the adult version, applied to the face. Men learn to give no reaction to a colleague's idea until they have decided what they think of it, to stay expressionless when a client pushes back, to receive praise and criticism with the same flat look.

The habit often starts as protection, and it often works. A face that gives nothing away cannot be used against you in a negotiation, cannot reveal panic in a crisis, cannot be accused of favouritism. In certain moments, as the last block of this chapter describes, those are real advantages.

The trouble is that most of working life is not a negotiation or a crisis. It is collaboration: people trying to understand each other, decide whom to trust and work out what is going on. In those settings, a face that shows nothing does not read as strength. It reads as nothing, and people fill the gap with their own guesses. The figure here stands at rest, face neutral. In a mirror, it looks composed. Across a meeting table, for an hour, it can look like disapproval, boredom or contempt.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's inexpressiveness at work were mostly a matter of temperament rather than learning. Temperament plays a part, and some people are naturally less expressive, but the norms of many workplaces clearly reward and teach composure.
teach.pullQuote: A face that shows nothing does not read as strength. It reads as nothing, and people fill the gap with guesses.

teach.p:
In 2003 Thomas Boone and Ross Buck argued that emotional expressivity evolved partly as a signal of cooperativeness. Because spontaneous expressions are hard to fake, they suggested, people who show their feelings give others evidence about their intentions, and others are right to trust them a little more.

Later studies have supported the idea. In 2010 Joanna Schug and her colleagues found that people who behaved cooperatively in economic games were more emotionally expressive than those who did not. In 2007 Eva Krumhuber and her colleagues found that people in a trust game trusted partners who smiled genuinely more than partners who did not, and trusted partners whose smiles looked fake less.

The point is not that every expressive person is trustworthy. Some are skilled at performing feeling, and the chapter on deception in Part I described how poorly anyone detects lies. The point is that a blank face gives other people no evidence at all, so they cannot calibrate their trust. In collaborative work, where people need to decide whom to rely on, that is a disadvantage.

The figure here listens attentively, his face responding to what he hears. Interest, surprise, amusement and concern pass across it as the speaker talks. To the speaker, those small movements are evidence that he is being heard by someone with a mind and a stake in the outcome. A still face, however attentive behind it, offers none of that evidence.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if expressive people were trusted no more than inexpressive ones. Studies of expressivity and cooperation mostly find an association, though the effect depends on whether expressions look genuine, and skilled performers can exploit it.

teach.h: Your face is other people's information.
teach.p:
The psychologist Gerben van Kleef has argued that emotions are a form of social information. People watch each other's faces to work out how things are going and what to do next. A colleague's smile says the idea is landing; a frown says it is not; a look of concern says something is wrong. People adjust their behaviour accordingly, often without noticing.

A manager with a poker face withholds that information from everyone around him. His team cannot tell whether he likes their work, whether a meeting went well, whether he is worried about the quarter or whether they are in trouble. And people do not respond to missing information neutrally. As the chapter on silence described, gaps tend to be filled with the worst available interpretation. A blank face after a presentation is read as disappointment. A blank face in a one-to-one is read as dissatisfaction.

The result is often the opposite of what the poker face was meant to achieve. People stop bringing problems, because they cannot predict the reaction. They over-prepare, second-guess and look elsewhere for signs of how they are doing. Good news is delivered late, and bad news later still.

The figure here sits back with arms folded, face neutral. He may be thinking hard, approving, tired or quietly pleased. Nobody in the room can tell, and so each of them is likely to decide, privately, that he is unimpressed.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people treated an unreadable face as neutral rather than filling the gap with interpretations. Research on emotions as social information and on ambiguity suggests they do not, though how they fill the gap depends on the relationship and the setting.

teach.p:
If showing more is generally better, is a big smile always best? Not quite. In 2017 Ze Wang and his colleagues showed people photographs of marketers and service providers smiling slightly or broadly. Broad smiles made them seem warmer but less competent than slight smiles. The trade-off mattered most when the stakes were high: when people were choosing a service where mistakes would be costly, competence counted for more, and the broad smile cost more.

The researchers also looked at crowdfunding pages and found that creators with broader smiles in their profile photos tended to raise less money, though that analysis was observational.

Other research points the other way. The study of video backgrounds described in the chapter on camera height found that smiling made people seem both more trustworthy and more competent. The difference may lie in intensity: a warm, moderate smile seems to help on both counts, while a very broad, beaming smile in a serious setting may tip toward seeming less competent.

For men who have trained themselves out of smiling at work, the practical message is to turn the dial up from zero, not to beam. A real, moderate smile when greeting someone, when an idea is good or when something is funny adds warmth without costing authority. In high-stakes moments, such as presenting to a board or delivering a diagnosis, a slight smile and a steady face may serve better. The figure here stands open and at ease. Warmth does not need a grin.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if smile intensity made no difference to judgments of warmth and competence. Wang and colleagues found a trade-off, but other studies find that moderate smiles help on both counts, so treat the effect as dependent on intensity and context.

teach.h: When the face is wrong for the moment.
teach.p:
Sometimes the trouble is not too little expression but the wrong one. In 2015 Leanne ten Brinke and Gabrielle Adams studied video of executives making public apologies for corporate failures, coding their facial expressions frame by frame, and compared them with how their companies' share prices moved afterwards. Executives who smiled while apologising tended to see their share prices do worse than expected. Executives who looked genuinely sad tended to see the damage contained.

In a follow-up experiment, people watched an actor playing an airline chief executive apologising for a computer failure that had stranded thousands of passengers. When he looked sad, viewers judged him as more sincere and were more willing to keep doing business with the company than when he smiled or looked neutral.

The finding fits the chapter on apology in Part III: an apology is judged by the body delivering it. A smile during an apology may be meant as warmth or as nerves, but it reads as not taking the harm seriously. A poker face reads much the same way.

The broader lesson is that expression is not a dial to be set once. It must fit the moment. Concern when someone brings bad news, pleasure when they bring good, seriousness when you are apologising, warmth when you are welcoming. The figures here show a man coming to apologise, hand on his chest and head lowered, to someone whose arms are still folded. A smile here would undo the words.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if facial expression during an apology made no difference to how it was received. ten Brinke and Adams found differences, though in a small sample of real apologies whose market effects have many causes, and in one experiment.

teach.h: The cost of acting all day.
teach.p:
Holding a professional face hour after hour is work. The sociologist Arlie Hochschild called it emotional labour: managing what you show, and sometimes what you feel, as part of a job. In 2003 Alicia Grandey distinguished two ways of doing it. Surface acting means changing your expression without changing your feeling: smiling while angry, looking calm while anxious, keeping a poker face while upset. Deep acting means changing the feeling itself, for example by seeing the situation differently, so that the expression follows.

In her study of service workers, surface acting was linked to stress, and colleagues rated the workers who relied on it as worse at delivering service with genuine warmth. Deep acting was linked to better ratings and was not linked to stress. Later research has repeatedly connected surface acting with emotional exhaustion, one of the dimensions of burnout described in Part II.

For a man who keeps a mask on all day, this is a warning. The effort of suppressing every reaction does not disappear; it accumulates. The chapter on the mask in Part II described how suppression raises physiological stress and makes partners in conversation uncomfortable. At work, it can also drain the energy you need for everything else.

The alternative is not to show every feeling, but to do less surface acting: to let genuine reactions show where they help, and where composure is needed, to work on the feeling itself, as the chapter on reappraisal in Part VI described, rather than only on the face. The figure here has slumped at the end of a long day. Some of that tiredness is the work. Some of it is the face.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if surface acting carried no cost compared with deep acting. Grandey and later research link surface acting to stress and exhaustion, though most of the evidence comes from service jobs and relies on self-report.

teach.p:
None of this means abandoning composure. There are moments when a still face is exactly right: in a negotiation, when an opponent makes an offer and you need time to think, as the chapter on negotiation later in this part describes; in a crisis, when panic would spread, as the chapter on high-stakes environments described; when you hold information you cannot share; or when someone tells you something shocking and needs you not to react.

The skill is choosing. Let your face show interest, appreciation, amusement and concern in ordinary collaboration, because those are the reactions that build trust and tell people where they stand. Save the poker face for the moments that need it. And when you are holding back, say so, so that the gap is not filled with guesses: “I'm keeping my reaction to myself until I've thought about this properly” is far better than a stony silence.

Ask how you come across. Many men with a strong poker face have no idea how forbidding it looks, and colleagues rarely say. A trusted colleague, or a recording of yourself in a meeting, as the chapter on video review described, will show you.

And as a reader, be fair to others' faces. Some people are naturally less expressive because of temperament, culture, neurodivergence or experience, and a still face from them may carry no message at all. The figures here stand angled toward each other in conversation. Between colleagues who can read each other's faces, a great deal is settled without a word.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if selective expressiveness produced no better outcomes than constant composure. The evidence on expressivity and trust supports it, though the right balance differs between workplaces and cultures.

caseStudy:
Mark, forty-four, is finance director of a manufacturing firm. He spent his twenties on a trading floor, where a face that gave nothing away was a survival skill, and he still prides himself on it. In his annual 360-degree review, the comments are consistent: excellent judgement, but impossible to read. One says that people rehearse for days before taking a problem to him, because they cannot predict how he will react.

The point is driven home when Mark announces a round of redundancies. He delivers the news calmly and precisely, with no visible emotion, because he does not want to make a hard moment harder. Afterwards he learns that staff are furious: many describe him as cold and indifferent. In fact he had slept badly for a week.

With a coach, Mark watches a recording of himself in a budget meeting. His face barely moves for forty minutes, even when a junior analyst presents work he privately thinks is excellent. He starts small. He lets himself smile when an idea is good, and says so. When people bring him bad news, he lets concern show before he asks questions. When he needs time to think, he says, “I'm going to keep my reaction to myself until I've looked at the numbers.”

He keeps his poker face for the quarterly meetings with the bank, where it still serves him well. Six months later, his team begins bringing him problems earlier, and the analyst whose work he praised tells him it was the first time she had known what he thought of anything she had done.
observe: In your next meeting, notice whose faces you can read and whose you cannot, and how that affects what you say to them.
Notice your own face during a colleague's presentation, and whether your reactions reach it.
Notice how people respond when someone's face stays blank after they have spoken.
Notice moments when composure clearly helped, and moments when it was mistaken for coldness.

drills.name: Watch Your Face
steps: Record yourself, with permission, during a meeting or a practice conversation.
Watch with the sound off and count the moments your face visibly reacted.
Note moments where you felt something but your face showed nothing.
Ask a trusted colleague how readable you seem, and write down what they say.
Choose one kind of reaction, such as appreciation, to let show more often.
variations: Watch a recording of yourself with the sound off and mark every moment when you think your face showed appreciation, then ask a colleague to mark the same moments independently.
Record yourself at home during a family meal, with everyone's agreement, and compare how readable your face is there and at work.
Count, during one meeting, how often your face reacts to junior colleagues compared with senior ones.

drills.name: Turn the Dial Up
steps: For one day, let a moderate, genuine smile show when you greet people and when something is good or funny.
Let concern show when someone brings you a problem, before you start solving it.
Write down one difference you noticed by the end of the day.
variations: For one day, tell three people specifically what you appreciated about something they did, and let your face show it as you say it.
Let one moment of genuine amusement show in a meeting where you would normally keep a straight face, and notice whether the room relaxes.
When someone brings you a problem, let your first expression be concern for them, not for the problem, and notice the difference.

drills.name: Name the Hold
steps: Write a sentence you can use when you need to hold back a reaction, such as “I'm keeping my reaction until I've thought about it.”
Use it the next time you need time to think.
Notice whether it changes how the other person behaves.
Adjust the wording until it sounds like you.
variations: Write three versions of your hold sentence, for a meeting, a negotiation and a conversation at home, and practise each aloud.
Use a hold sentence the next time someone surprises you with bad news, then come back to them within a day with your view, as promised.
Ask a colleague how it felt when you named a hold, compared with times when you simply went quiet.

drills.name: Fit the Moment
steps: List four situations you face at work: good news, bad news, an apology, a negotiation.
For each, write the expression that fits: warmth, concern, seriousness, composure.
Note which one you find hardest to show.
Practise that expression in front of a mirror or camera until it feels natural.
Use it the next time the situation arises.
variations: Add two situations from your home life to the list, such as a child's bad news or a partner's good news, and choose the expression that fits each.
Watch a news clip of a public apology with the sound off and judge whether the face fits the moment, then check your judgment with the sound on.
Before your next difficult conversation, decide in advance which expression you want the other person to see first.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a face which gives nothing away makes you seem more professional and trustworthy. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; inexpressive people are trusted most in every workplace
Expressive people tend to be trusted more; a blank face gives others no evidence
Expressiveness matters only in sales roles, not in other kinds of work
Trust depends entirely on what people say, and never on what their faces happen to show
quiz.explain: Research inspired by Boone and Buck links expressivity with cooperation and trust, and genuine smiles draw more trust than fake ones. A blank face offers no evidence to calibrate trust, so people fill the gap with guesses.

quiz.q: What did Wang and colleagues find about broad and slight smiles?
options: Broad smiles made people seem warmer but less competent than slight smiles
Broad smiles made people seem both warmer and more competent in all cases
Slight smiles made people seem colder and less competent than the broad smiles did
Smile intensity made no difference to judgments of warmth or competence
quiz.explain: Broad smiles raised warmth but lowered perceived competence, especially when stakes were high. A moderate, genuine smile avoids most of the trade-off.

quiz.q: What did ten Brinke and Adams find about executives' expressions during corporate apologies?
options: Executives with neutral faces protected their companies best of all
Expressions made no difference to how markets responded to apologies
Executives who smiled saw better results, because they seemed calm and confident
Smiling while apologising tended to go with worse outcomes than sadness
quiz.explain: Executives who smiled during apologies tended to see their share prices do worse, while those who looked sad tended to contain the damage. The expression must fit the moment.

quiz.q: According to Grandey's research, how did surface acting compare with deep acting?
options: Surface acting was linked to stress and to worse ratings of warm service
Surface acting was linked to less stress and to better ratings of warm service
Both forms of acting had identical effects on stress and service quality
Deep acting was linked to stress, while surface acting had no effect
quiz.explain: Changing only the expression was linked to stress and to colleagues rating service as less genuinely warm, while changing the feeling itself was linked to better ratings. Later research connects surface acting with exhaustion.

quiz.q: A junior colleague presents work you think is excellent. Your habit is to keep a neutral face and say nothing until later. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep the neutral face, so that she does not become complacent
Wait until her annual review to tell her what you thought of it
Let your appreciation show, and tell her now what you thought of it
Give her a broad grin and a thumbs-up, but say nothing about the work itself
quiz.explain: A blank face after a presentation is usually read as disappointment. Letting genuine appreciation show, and saying so, gives her the information she needs and builds trust.

quiz.q: In a negotiation, the other side makes an offer far lower than you expected. What does this chapter suggest about your face?
options: Let your shock show fully, so they know the offer is unacceptable
This is a moment where composure helps; keep a calm face and take time to think
Smile broadly, so that they think you are pleased with the offer
Laugh at the offer, so that they realise how unrealistic it is
quiz.explain: Selective expressiveness keeps composure for moments that need it, and a negotiation is one of them. Saying you need time to think avoids the gap being filled with guesses.

quiz.q: Why did Boone and Buck suggest that expressive people may be trusted more?
options: Because expressive people are usually more senior and therefore more experienced
Because spontaneous expressions are hard to fake, so they give evidence of intentions
Because expressive people talk more and so other people simply get to know them faster
Because people trust anyone who smiles a lot, whatever their behaviour turns out to be
quiz.explain: Boone and Buck argued that expressivity evolved partly as a signal of cooperativeness. Spontaneous expressions are hard to fake, so they give others evidence about what a person intends.

quiz.q: A calm, experienced officer takes a statement from an elderly burglary victim with a steady, unmoving face. She later says he did not care. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep the same face next time, since calm is always the most professional choice
Let concern show inside the calm, and acknowledge her distress before the forms
Become visibly upset with her, so that she can see exactly how much he cares
Ignore the complaint, since victims often blame officers for things they cannot change
quiz.explain: Calm helps in a crisis, but a frightened person also needs to see that their distress has registered. Concern shown within composure matches the moment without adding to her fear.

quiz.q: Someone says that what your face shows at work is your own business and has no effect on anyone else. What does van Kleef's work suggest?
options: That other people use your expressions as information about how things are going and what to do next
That faces at work are mostly ignored, since people pay attention only to what is actually said aloud
That expressions matter only in face-to-face sales, where customers watch the seller very carefully
That people read faces only when they already know the person well, and never in the first meetings
quiz.explain: Van Kleef argues that emotions act as social information. Colleagues read your face to judge how their work and the meeting are going, and adjust their behaviour accordingly.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific situation at work where your face, or lack of expression, was misread: as cold, disapproving, bored or indifferent. What were you actually feeling, and what did others see? Where did you learn to keep your face still? Then think of one setting where composure genuinely helps you. Describe one reaction you will let show more often, and one moment where you will keep your poker face and explain that you are doing so.
reflection.guidance: Many men only discover how unreadable they are through feedback or a recording, so if you can, watch yourself before you write. Be specific about the reaction you will let show and the words you will use when you hold back. The aim is not to perform emotion but to stop hiding the ones that would help.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat a blank face as neutral, when people fill the gap with the worst available interpretation: disapproval, boredom or contempt. The second is to hide genuine appreciation and concern, so that colleagues cannot tell where they stand and stop bringing you problems. The third is to swing to the opposite extreme, beaming broadly in high-stakes settings where a moderate expression would serve better. The fourth is to show the wrong expression for the moment, such as smiling while apologising or staying blank while delivering bad news. And the fifth is to surface act all day, suppressing every reaction, and pay for it in exhaustion. Show what helps, keep composure for the moments that need it, and say when you are holding back.

moreCases.title: The new manager who kept his cards close
moreCases.scene:
Raj, thirty-four, was the best engineer on his team for six years, and in January he was promoted to lead it. He has never managed anyone
  before. The manager he most admired, his first boss, was a calm, quiet man who never raised his voice and never seemed rattled, and Raj has
  decided to manage the same way. In his weekly one-to-ones with his seven engineers, he listens carefully, asks precise questions, takes notes
  and keeps his face still. He does not want to seem to have favourites, and he does not want to react before he has thought.

  By April, the one-to-ones have become strangely quiet. People bring him finished work but not problems. When something goes wrong, he hears about
  it late, usually from someone outside the team. Chloe, the most experienced engineer, who was also considered for his job, has started to give
  short answers and leave early.

  Then a recruiter's message to Chloe is forwarded to Raj by mistake. She has been talking to another company for a month. In the exit
  conversation that follows, he asks her, as calmly as he can, what went wrong. She says she never had any idea what he thought of her work. Every
  time she showed him something, his face stayed exactly the same, and she had come to assume that meant he was disappointed.

  Raj is stunned. He had thought her work was the best on the team. He had said, in her last one-to-one, that it was "fine", and meant it as high
  praise.

Raj has also noticed that the team's chat channel goes quiet when he joins a conversation, and that jokes that were flying around a moment earlier stop. He has put it down to the normal distance between a manager and a team.

In team meetings it is the same. When someone proposes an idea, Raj listens with the same level expression whether he likes it or not, and then asks a careful question. The engineers have learned to read the question as the verdict, and to brace for it.
moreCases.misread:
Chloe read Raj's still face and his careful "fine" as disappointment, and the rest of the team read them as a reason to keep problems to themselves. Raj read the quiet one-to-ones as a sign that the team was running smoothly.

He also read his own stillness as fairness, when to the team it looked like a judgment that never came.

Raj also missed the quiet signals his team sent back: the shorter one-to-ones, the problems that arrived late, the senior engineer who stopped staying for a chat at the end. He read each one, if he noticed it at all, as a sign of efficiency.
moreCases.betterRead:
Van Kleef's view of emotions as social information explains what happened. People watch a manager's face to find out how they are doing and what to do next. Raj's still face withheld that information, and his team filled the gap in the worst way available. Composure had been his old boss's style, but his old boss, Raj later remembered, also laughed easily and said "That's great" when he meant it. Raj's better approach was to keep his calm but let his reactions show. He started telling people specifically what he liked about their work, letting his face show interest when they brought problems, and saying "Give me a minute to think" when he needed one. Chloe left, but two months later the team's one-to-ones were full of problems again, brought early.

He also told the team, at the next meeting, that he had realised his face was hard to read, and that if they ever wanted to know what he thought, they should ask. Several did.

moreCases.title: The officer at the door
moreCases.scene:
Dave, forty-eight, is a police constable with twenty years' service, most of it in a busy town centre. He prides himself on staying calm.
  He has been to fights, crashes and worse, and he has learned to keep his face steady and his voice even, because panic spreads and someone has to
  be the still point. Colleagues say he is the person you want beside you when things go wrong.

  One Tuesday morning he is sent to a house where an elderly woman, Margaret, eighty-one, has come home from a hospital appointment to find her back
  door forced and her bedroom ransacked. Her late husband's watch and her wedding jewellery have gone. When Dave arrives she is sitting at the
  kitchen table, shaking, with a neighbour holding her hand.

  Dave is thorough. He takes a full statement, checks the door, photographs the bedroom, gives her a crime reference number and a leaflet about
  victim support, and tells her honestly that the chances of recovering the jewellery are not high. His face stays calm and level throughout. He is
  in the house for forty minutes.

  A week later, Margaret's son makes a complaint. His mother, he writes, felt that the officer "couldn't have cared less" and treated her "like a
  piece of paperwork". She has not slept properly since. Dave's sergeant, who has worked with him for years, reads the complaint and knows it is not
  true, but she also knows that it is how it felt.

Dave's colleagues, when they hear about the complaint, are indignant on his behalf. One of them says the old lady should be grateful he turned up at all, given how stretched the shift was. Dave says nothing, but he goes over the visit in his head for days.

In the car afterwards, Dave had thought about his own mother, who is about Margaret's age, and how she would feel coming home to a forced door. He had felt it keenly. None of it reached his face.
moreCases.misread:
Margaret read Dave's steady, unmoving face as indifference: to her loss, to her fear and to her. Dave read his own calm as professionalism and kindness, the right way to help someone who was already frightened.

And Dave read the complaint, when he first heard of it, as ingratitude, which hurt him more than he showed.

The colleagues who defended him read the complaint as an attack on the job, and so missed what it said about how the visit had felt to someone frightened and alone. Margaret's son read Dave's calm as a lack of respect for his mother.
moreCases.betterRead: Calm helps in a crisis, but a frightened or grieving person also needs to see that their distress has registered. Ten Brinke and Adams found that executives who looked genuinely sad when apologising did better than those who smiled; a face that matches the moment tells people they have been understood. Dave's composure was right for a fight in the street and wrong for a widow at her kitchen table. His sergeant's better advice was not to stop being steady but to let concern show inside the steadiness: to sit down at her level, to say "I'm so sorry, this is a horrible thing to come home to," and to let his face say it too, before turning to the forms. Dave went back to see Margaret, with her son's agreement. He told her he was sorry she had felt that way. She said, "You seemed nicer this time." He said he had been just as sorry the first time, and that he had not shown it.

moreCases.title: The adviser who smiled at everything
moreCases.scene:
Jamie, twenty-nine, is a financial adviser at a small firm that helps people plan for retirement. He is cheerful, likeable and good at his
  job, and he has been told since school that his smile is his best feature. He uses it. He smiles broadly when clients arrive, when he explains
  their options, when he goes through the risks and when they sign.

  His clients like him, and his first meetings go well. But fewer of them come back to invest than come back for his older colleague, Susan, who
  is quieter and smiles less. When Jamie asks his manager why, she shows him the feedback from a recent survey of clients who chose not to proceed.
  Several describe him as "lovely" and "very friendly". One says she was not sure he understood how serious the decision was for her. Another writes:
  "Nice lad, but I wanted someone who would worry about my money as much as I do."

  Jamie is hurt. He thought his smile showed that he was confident and on their side. He watches Susan in a meeting with a couple in their sixties who
  are deciding what to do with a pension. She smiles warmly when they arrive. When she talks about the risks, her face is serious and still, and she
  pauses to let them take in each one. When they make their decision, she smiles again.

Jamie's manager also mentions, kindly, that he smiled throughout a meeting in which a widow explained that she needed to plan her finances because her husband had died. She had found it difficult to say, and had mentioned it in her feedback.

When he thinks about it honestly, Jamie realises that he smiles most when he is least sure of himself. The bigger the number on the page, the wider the smile.
moreCases.misread:
Jamie's clients read his constant broad smile as friendliness and, in a high-stakes decision, as a lack of seriousness about their money. Jamie read his own smile as reassurance, and did not notice that it never changed with the subject.

Susan's quieter clients might have read Jamie's grin as nerves, if they had thought about it, and they would have been closer to the truth. Several simply decided, without quite knowing why, that they would rather trust their savings to someone who seemed to take them more seriously. Jamie, for his part, read their decisions as bad luck.
moreCases.betterRead:
Wang and colleagues found that broad smiles made people seem warmer but less competent than slight ones, and that the cost was greatest when the stakes were high. A pension is about as high-stakes as most people's decisions get. Susan's face moved with the conversation: warm for the welcome, serious for the risks, warm again for the decision. That movement told her clients that she understood what each moment meant to them. Jamie's better approach was not to stop smiling but to let his smile follow the subject. He practised keeping a moderate, warm expression for greetings and a serious, attentive one for risks and losses. Six months later his clients' survey comments still said "friendly", and several now said "careful".

He also learned to stop smiling when a client talked about a loss, a death or a fear, and simply to listen with his face still and his eyes on theirs. Those were the moments, he later said, when clients decided to trust him.

moreCases.title: The front-desk smile
moreCases.scene:
Leah, thirty-one, manages the front desk of a large hotel near an airport. Her shifts are ten hours long, and for most of them she is on show:
  checking guests in, handling complaints about rooms and delayed flights, calming people who have been travelling for a day and want someone to
  blame. The hotel trains its staff to smile at every guest, and Leah is very good at it. Guests often mention her by name in their reviews.

  Lately she has started to dread the end of her shifts. By the time she gets home she has nothing left. She snaps at her partner over small things,
  and on her days off she does not want to see anyone. She has begun to feel that her smile at work is a mask she puts on in the staff room and takes
  off in the car park, and that the person underneath it is getting more tired and less patient every month.

  One evening a guest whose flight has been cancelled shouts at her for ten minutes about the price of a room. She smiles throughout, apologises,
  finds him a cheaper rate and wishes him a good night. Then she goes into the back office and finds her hands are shaking.

  Her friend Noor, a nurse, listens to her describe it and says that it sounds like the kind of exhaustion she sees in colleagues on difficult
  wards.

She has tried to talk to her manager about it, but he praised her smile and said she was a natural. She did not know how to say that being a natural was exactly what was exhausting her.

She has noticed something else. The guests she finds easiest are the ones she genuinely likes, the tired families and the nervous first-time travellers, and those shifts leave her far less drained than the ones spent smiling at people who are rude to her.
moreCases.misread:
Leah read her exhaustion as a personal weakness: a sign that she was not cut out for the job, or that she was becoming an unpleasant person. She read her smile as the professional part of her, and her tiredness as the problem.

Her manager read the same smile as proof that she loved the job, and so missed every sign that she was struggling.

And she read the shaking hands after the shouting guest as a failure of nerve, when they were the ordinary aftermath of ten minutes of holding a smile over fear and anger.
moreCases.betterRead:
Grandey found that surface acting, changing your expression without changing your feeling, was linked to emotional exhaustion, while deep acting, changing the feeling itself, was not linked to it in the same way. Leah had spent years smiling over anger, fear and frustration, and the gap between her face and her feelings was costing her. Her better path combined several changes. With Noor's help she began to reappraise some encounters, seeing the shouting guest as a frightened man stranded far from home, which made a sympathetic expression easier to mean. She asked her manager for a rule that staff could hand over an abusive guest to a colleague. And she stopped smiling at people who were shouting at her, keeping instead a calm, serious face that matched the moment. She still went home tired, but not empty.

Noor was careful to say that if the exhaustion did not lift, Leah should see her doctor, and Leah did, to rule out anything else.

The change in her face was small, but she noticed the difference by the end of the first week.

workedReading.title: Reviewing a junior's work in front of a client
workedReading.scene:
Andrew, forty-seven, is a partner at an architecture practice. On Thursday he has two meetings about the same project, a new library for a small town. In the morning, his junior architect, Mei, twenty-six, will show him her first full design for the building. In the afternoon, they will present it to the town council's committee, who will also want to talk about the budget, which has gone up. Andrew is known in the practice for his poker face. He learned it from the partner who trained him, who said that clients should never see you surprised. He has started to wonder, after a colleague's comment at the practice away-day, whether his juniors find him as unreadable as his clients do. He decides to use Thursday to practise choosing what his face shows, rather than showing nothing all day by default.

He has also noticed, over the years, that the juniors who work with him most closely tend to over-prepare for his reviews, bringing three versions of every drawing in case he dislikes the first. He has always taken it as diligence. He now wonders whether it is anxiety, and whether his face is the reason.

He wants to see whether a face can be both trusted by a committee and readable to a junior, or whether he has to choose.

steps.label: Notice your default
steps.text:
Before Mei arrives, Andrew looks at his reflection in the dark screen of his laptop. His resting face is serious, a little stern, with his lips pressed together. He knows that this is the face he wears for most of the day, and that it has served him well in negotiations and difficult site meetings. He also knows that, from across a desk, it could easily look like disapproval. He reminds himself that a blank face is not neutral to the person looking at it.

He thinks, too, about how the review usually goes. He looks at each drawing in silence, for a long time, and then gives his verdict. To him the silence is concentration. To the person across the desk it must feel like waiting for a sentence.

steps.label: Decide what to show
steps.text:
He thinks about what Mei needs from the review. She needs to know which parts of the design work and which do not, and she needs to leave confident enough to present it to a committee in a few hours. He decides that he will let his appreciation show where he feels it, show concern only where he has it, and keep his reaction to himself on anything he needs time to think about.

He also decides what he will not do. He will not fake enthusiasm for parts of the design he does not like, because Mei would hear the falseness, and it would make his praise worth less.

And he reminds himself that the purpose of the review is to make the building better, not to test Mei's nerve. His face should serve that purpose.

steps.label: Let appreciation show first
steps.text:
Mei opens the drawings. The reading room, lit from above through a long roof light, is very good, and he lets himself smile and lean forward. "That's lovely," he says. "The light in there is exactly right." He watches her shoulders drop a little. Van Kleef's work suggests that she will use his face as information about how she is doing. He wants it to tell her the truth, and the truth here is good.

He goes on to name two more things he likes, specifically: the way the entrance draws people in from the market square, and the choice of timber. Specific praise tells her that he has looked closely, which is part of what makes it believable.

steps.label: Name the hold
steps.text:
The children's section is more of a puzzle. He is not sure the layout will work for buggies, but he wants to look again before he says so. Instead of a blank face, which she might read as disapproval, he says, "I want to think about the children's area before I give you a view. Can we come back to it at the end?" She nods. Naming the hold means she does not have to guess what his silence means.

It costs him nothing to say, and it changes what his silence means while he studies the drawings. Mei can now carry on presenting without trying to read his face for a verdict he has not reached.

steps.label: Show concern without alarm
steps.text:
When they return to the children's area, he shows her the problem with the buggies, and lets his face show concern, a slight frown and a serious look, but not alarm. He suggests a fix. She sees it at once and sketches it. His face relaxes again, and he tells her it is better than his suggestion, which is true.

The concern is about the drawing, not about her, and he makes sure his face says so. When she looks worried, he smiles and says, "This is exactly what reviews are for." The frown goes as soon as the problem is solved, so that it does not hang over the rest of the meeting.

Mei says later that the frown was useful: it told her the problem mattered, and the smile that followed told her it was solved.

steps.label: Keep composure for the committee
steps.text:
In the afternoon, the committee's chair says that the budget increase is unacceptable and that they may have to look at other practices. Andrew keeps his face still and his voice level. This is the moment for composure: he needs time to think, and surprise or irritation would weaken his position. He says, "I understand. Let me take you through where the increase comes from," and does. When Mei presents the reading room, he lets his pride in her show, because it is real and it helps the committee trust the work.

After the meeting, the chair stays behind to shake his hand and says that he liked the way Andrew had kept calm about the money while being so clearly proud of his team's work. Andrew notes that the two did not conflict.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The committee approves the design and agrees to look again at the budget with the practice. On the train home, Mei tells Andrew that the morning review was the most useful she has had. She says she had always found his reviews nerve-racking, because she could never tell what he thought until the end. Andrew writes three words in his notebook: appreciation, hold, composure. He resolves to use the poker face as a tool for particular moments, not as the face he wears all day.

He also notices that he feels less tired than usual at the end of a day of meetings, perhaps because he spent less of it holding his face still.

A month later, Mei brings him a problem with the structural drawings the day she spots it, rather than a week later with three possible solutions.

moreFailures.title: Carrying the work face home
moreFailures.body:
A face trained for the trading floor, the courtroom or the operating theatre does not always switch off at the front door. Many men find that the composure that serves them at work follows them into the kitchen, so that a partner who tells them about a hard day, or a child who brings home a bad mark, meets the same still, assessing face that their colleagues see. At home that face is read even more harshly than at work, because the people there expect to see warmth. Children, in particular, may read a parent's blank face as disappointment and stop bringing their problems. The chapter on the "I'm fine" mask in Part II described the costs of habitual suppression to close relationships. If you notice that the people at home have started to tell you less, ask whether they can read you, and let your face come home too.

It can help to mark the change between work and home with a small ritual: a walk, a change of clothes, a few minutes in the car before you go in. Some men find that it gives the work face somewhere to stay.

moreFailures.title: Faking the expression instead of finding the feeling
moreFailures.body:
Once people learn that expressiveness builds trust, some try to manufacture it: a fixed smile in meetings, a practised look of concern, a nod at every point. It tends to backfire twice. Others often sense that the expression does not fit, and Krumhuber and colleagues found that smiles which looked fake reduced trust rather than building it. And Grandey's research suggests that surface acting of this kind is tiring, linked to emotional exhaustion in a way that genuine feeling is not. The better route is usually to find the feeling that belongs to the moment. Look for what you do genuinely appreciate in a colleague's work, or what genuinely concerns you about a problem, and let that show. If you feel nothing, say something true instead of performing something false.

A useful rule is never to show a feeling you do not have, and to look for the feelings you do have but usually hide. Most people find there are plenty of the second kind.

If a colleague's work leaves you cold, say what would make it better, with a face that shows you want it to succeed.

moreFailures.title: Saving your warmth for the people above you
moreFailures.body:
Some men are readable and warm with their bosses, their clients and anyone senior, and still and unreadable with the people who report to them. The pattern is often unconscious: warmth is offered upwards, where it is felt to matter, and withheld downwards, where composure is felt to signal authority. But the people below notice, and they read it accurately as a statement about whom you value. It also robs them of the information they most need, because a junior colleague depends far more on your face to know how they are doing than your boss does. Watch yourself for a day and notice whom you smile at. If your warmth flows only upwards, your team will learn to keep their problems from you, as Raj's did.

The same pattern can run along other lines too: warmth for people who look and sound like you, stillness for those who do not. It is worth checking for both.

Ask yourself who last saw you laugh at work, and who has never seen it.

moreFailures.title: Mistaking a still face for emotional control
moreFailures.body:
A still face can feel like control, but hiding a feeling is not the same as managing it. The irritation, worry or hurt is still there, and it tends to leak out elsewhere: in a clipped email later, in impatience with the next person, in sleepless nights or in a sudden flash of anger that surprises everyone, because nobody saw it coming. The chapter on the "I'm fine" mask described research by Gross and John suggesting that people who habitually hide their feelings report lower wellbeing than people who more often reappraise the situation. Real emotional control includes noticing what you feel, naming it to yourself and deciding what to do with it. Sometimes that means keeping it off your face for now. It should rarely mean pretending, even to yourself, that it is not there.

If you find that feelings you have kept off your face keep coming back as sleeplessness, irritability or low mood, talk to someone about them, and if they persist, see your doctor.

Noticing a feeling and choosing not to show it for now is control. Refusing to notice it at all is not.

questions.q: Isn't showing emotion at work unprofessional?
questions.a:
It depends on which emotion, how much and when. Shouting, sulking and visible contempt are unprofessional, and nobody is suggesting you bring them to work. But appreciation, interest, concern and amusement are not unprofessional; they are a large part of what makes people trust and work well with you. Boone and Buck argued that expressive people give others evidence about their intentions, and later studies suggested that people who behave cooperatively tend to be more expressive. A face that never moves withholds that evidence. Professionalism means choosing what to show and when, not showing nothing at all, and the people who are best at it usually show a good deal of moderate, genuine feeling.

And the moments when composure matters most, a crisis, a negotiation, a shock, are easier to handle if people already know what your face looks like when you are pleased.

In most workplaces, the people others most want to work for are both composed and readable.

questions.q: How do I show appreciation without seeming gushing?
questions.a:
Be specific and moderate. A short, genuine smile with a precise comment, such as "The way you set out the options made that decision easy," says far more than a broad grin and "Brilliant, amazing, love it." Specific praise shows that you have paid attention, which is what most people want. Let your face match your words rather than exceed them, and say it at the moment, not three weeks later in an appraisal. If you have been reserved for years, the first few times will feel like too much to you and will almost certainly look like very little to others. Ask a trusted colleague whether it registered, and adjust.

And remember that appreciation is most useful when it is about something the person did, not about the person in general.

Gushing usually comes from praising everything; if your appreciation is selective and specific, it will rarely seem excessive.

questions.q: What if my face naturally looks stern?
questions.a:
Many people's resting faces look more serious, tired or cross than they feel, because of the shape of their brows, mouth or jaw. You cannot change your face, and you should not have to smile all day to make up for it. What you can do is make sure that your face moves when something happens: a small smile when someone arrives, raised brows when they say something interesting, a softening when they bring you a problem. You can also use words to fill the gap: "I'm really pleased with this, even if my face doesn't always say so." People who know about your resting face quickly learn to read past it, especially if you tell them.

It also helps to know how your face looks on video, where a stern resting face can seem sterner still, as the chapters on calls earlier in this part describe.

questions.q: How can I keep a straight face in a negotiation without seeming cold?
questions.a:
Be warm before and after, and composed during. Greet people properly, show interest in them and their position, and let your face be readable while you are building the relationship. When an offer arrives, or a moment comes when you need time to think, keep your face still and say so: "Let me think about that." Naming the hold stops the other side from reading your stillness as contempt or as a bluff. Then return to warmth when the moment passes. The chapter on the negotiation table later in this part describes how composure and warmth can work together, and why there are no reliable tells to hide in the first place.

It also helps to let colleagues see you laugh at your own resting face. Once it becomes a shared joke, it stops being a mystery.

And when the deal is done, let your face show what you feel about it, whether that is satisfaction, relief or respect for a hard bargain. People remember the end of a negotiation.

questions.q: Can I learn to be more expressive if I have been reserved all my life?
questions.a:
Yes, though it usually starts on the inside rather than the outside. Levant argued that many boys are taught to stop noticing and naming soft feelings, and if that happened to you, the first step is to notice what you feel at all. Try naming one feeling a day to yourself, at the moment you feel it. Then let a little of it show, starting with the easiest feelings, such as appreciation or amusement, with the people you trust most. Watch how they respond. Expressiveness is partly a habit, and habits change with practice. Most men who try this find that the change looks much smaller from outside than it feels from inside, and that people respond to it warmly.

Some men find it easier to start with other people's feelings than their own: noticing what a colleague might be feeling and saying so, which builds the same muscles from a safer angle.

questions.q: Is the trade-off different for women at work?
questions.a:
In some ways, yes. The chapter on the nonverbal glass ceiling later in this part describes research suggesting that observers judge the same expressions differently depending on who shows them, for example that anger can raise a man's perceived status and lower a woman's. That means the dial described here may be read differently for women, and that much of the problem lies with the people doing the reading rather than the person being read. If you evaluate others, the most useful thing this chapter can offer is to check your own reactions to other people's faces, and ask whether you would read the same expression the same way on someone else.

It also means that advice to women to smile more, or less, at work often misses the point. The fairer fix is in how expressions are judged.

If you are a man who is read as more authoritative when you are stern, it is worth knowing that the same face might cost a female colleague, and adjusting how you read hers.

watch.title: Rounders: Spotting KGB's Tell
watch.notice: A poker player realises that his opponent gives away his hand through the way he eats a biscuit. A film version of the tell; the chapter explains why a poker face at work often costs more trust than it protects.

reviewPrompt: This week, let one genuine reaction show in each meeting, and when you need to hold back, say that you are doing so.
